2027 Hyundai Elantra & 2028 Elantra Hybrid: How Do They Compare to Other Affordable Compact Sedans?
11 photos
Photo: Hyundai
The eighth generation of the ubiquitous compact and affordable sedan has arrived in front of the global audience at the 2026 Los Angeles Auto Show . And no, you’re not having déjà vu, as the model has already been shown before as the KDM-specification Hyundai Avante back in June during the Busan International Mobility Show at home in South Korea.
Now, the compact sedan series with many names – it’s known as the Hyundai Elantra globally and in North America specifically, but also as the i30 Sedan in Australia, besides Avante at home in South Korea- introduces the bold Art of Steel design alongside the all-new Tucson. It also packs advanced connectivity and safety technology, as well as expanded passenger space because it’s larger.
Hyundai Motor America unveiled the all-new 2027 Elantra and 2028 Elantra Hybrid at AutoMobility LA 2026 at the Los Angeles Auto Show, introducing the latest iteration of one of the brand’s most successful and longest-running nameplates – the first generation launched in 1990, almost three decades ago.
Since passenger cars are currently in jeopardy due to the continued success of crossovers, SUVs, and trucks, Hyundai wanted to expand Elantra’s appeal “beyond traditional compact sedan expectations, (so) this all-new model pairs a bold and muscular look, closer to midsize-class passenger space, the Pleos Connect infotainment, and enhanced safety features.”
Photo: Hyundai It’s also available with both ICE and hybrid powertrains , with the longer wheelbase designed to provide “generous interior room approaching mid-size dimensions and best-in-class rear passenger space,” including 39.1 inches of rear legroom, and Pleos Connect, Hyundai’s new Android Automotive OS-based infotainment and connectivity hub, packs a 12.9-inch Full HD display and the Gleo AI voice assistant plus over-the-air update features.
Hyundai makes a statement with the design of the Elantra and Tucson , again reshuffling expectations, and the Elantra looks like an N model without actually paying the premium, if you ask us. That’s not a bad idea, since the competition may be dwindling, but it remains absolutely laser-focused, including in the United States.
What remains to be seen is whether Hyundai is going in the right direction with the design that is deeply connected between the Elantra and Tucson and probably upcoming new models, while the interior is now mostly the same, featuring the big central screen, the same dashboard layout, and a slim 9.9-inch digital instrument cluster display atop the dashboard, seen by the driver above, not through the steering wheel.
Photo: Hyundai Under the hood, though, Hyundai plays it safe – and according to the current preferences of customers. In the United States, Hyundai will introduce the 2027 Elantra ICE with the SE, SEL Sport, and Limited trim levels rocking the same 2.0-liter four-pot with front-wheel drive and 147 hp, along with a combined rating of up to 35 MPG.
All models are now 3.4 inches longer, 1.2 inches wider, and 0.4 inches taller for the ICE model, and feature a wheelbase that has grown by 1.2 inches compared to the outgoing model. As for the 2028 Hyundai Elantra Hybrid, which obviously has late 2027 availability, the grades include SE Blue, SEL Sport Hybrid, and Limited Hybrid trims with an electrified 1.6-liter engine packing a combined 155 hp and up to 53 MPG combined.
Importantly, the Elantra Hybrid will arrive with a better rear suspension – a multi-link independent setup versus ICE’s coupled torsion beam. Alas, that doesn’t mean that either will have an easy time across the US compact sedan segment when they arrive at dealerships.
Photo: Hyundai The competition is pretty stiff and offers quite a lot of options, actually. We start randomly with the Honda Civic, which just got updated for the 2027 model year with increased pricing (+$300 across the board) and a new Sport-L grade. The prices are not important at the moment since we don’t know the MSRPs from Hyundai, but the 2027 Honda Civic offers plenty of punch – the Sedan body style has a 2.0-liter with 150 hp for the ICE model, while the Civic Hybrid easily bests the Elantra Hybrid with its two-motor system with a combined 200 hp.
Next up comes the ubiquitous Toyota Corolla, which is well known for its iconic reliability and great hybrid powertrain – though it’s obviously way blander than the new Elantra, just like the Civic. Options include the regular Corolla 2.0L with 169 hp, while the hybrid model is less potent at 138 combined hp. We’re not done yet, by the way.
The Kia cousin has the new K4 on offer, which replaced the Forte with an equally bold design like the Elantra, plus the same base engine with 147 hp. Kia also boasts a more potent 1.6-liter turbo with 190 hp if you can’t wait for the Elantra N, but in turn doesn’t offer a hybrid option. The Nissan Sentra has been completely redesigned for the 2026 model year and packs a 2.0-liter with 149 hp and the Xtronic CVT, but again lacks a hybrid option.
Miscellaneous options also include the Mazda3, which is way sportier with a 2.5-liter in NA or turbo form with 186 or 250 hp, as well as the Volkswagen Jetta, a classic compact German sedan packing standard turbo powertrains for added sportiness – the 1.5-liter has 158 hp and the 2.0-liter rocks 228 ponies in GLI specification.
